analysis.one_liner: Limits secret court settlements that hide evidence of dangers to public health or safety.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee, held one subcommittee hearing in April 1994, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies get sued over dangerous products, they often settle on condition that the evidence stays sealed forever. This bill would have required federal judges to make specific findings before sealing court records or restricting what parties can disclose, and would have barred any settlement clause that stops a party from reporting information relevant to a civil case to federal or state regulators. Courts would also have to re-examine protective orders after a final judgment so hidden safety evidence could come out.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, patients, and workers who rely on courts to surface evidence about defective products, unsafe drugs, and workplace hazards. Regulators would also gain access to information that secrecy agreements currently keep from them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and workers exposed to hidden hazards

how_it_helps.text: Requires a judge to make particularized findings that a protective order or sealing order will not restrict disclosure of information relevant to public health or safety before entering it.

Bars settlement agreements in federal civil cases from containing any provision that prohibits a party from disclosing case-relevant information to a federal or state agency with enforcement authority over the activity involved.
Puts the burden of proof on the party seeking secrecy, and requires a separate finding before any protective order survives a final judgment.

analysis.who_pays: Companies facing product-liability and negligence lawsuits — makers of pharmaceuticals, vehicles, tires, industrial equipment, and consumer goods — would lose a tool for keeping adverse evidence out of public view and out of regulators' hands.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that protective orders protect genuinely confidential trade secrets and proprietary information; the bill does not eliminate those protections, but opponents contended the new findings requirements would raise litigation costs and make legitimate confidentiality harder to obtain.

Defendants and their counsel also argued that federal courts routinely handle these matters and that a uniform statutory rule could discourage settlements by making secrecy harder to promise, potentially prolonging litigation over dangerous products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a narrow, specific practice: using court secrecy to bury evidence about hazards to public health or safety. Its carve-outs for confidential information disclosed to agencies, and the requirement that judges make case-specific findings rather than banning secrecy outright, keep the cost to legitimate trade secrecy modest. The main trade-off is some added litigation friction for defendants; the main benefit is that dangers documented in court files would no longer be locked away by private agreement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent to its subcommittee on courts, got one hearing in April 1994, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 1993 on August 6, 1993, with introductory remarks in the Senate.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
In February 1994 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice, which held hearings on April 20, 1994.
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and received no vote in either chamber before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use sealed settlements and protective orders to keep evidence of safety hazards out of public view and away from regulators keep that ability. Consumers and workers are left with the same information gaps the bill aimed to close.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that keep lawsuit evidence sealed

for.name: Sen. Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks arguing for it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 103rd Congress by Sen. Joseph Biden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in August 1993, sent it to the Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice, held one hearing, and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Defense bar and business groups
against.role: Litigation defendants and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed limiting protective orders and sealed settlements, arguing the rules would raise litigation costs and undermine legitimate confidentiality; opposition helped keep the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Democratic cosponsor signed on and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split; the bill's sponsor and cosponsor were both Democrats.

industries.industry: Companies facing product-liability lawsuits (pharmaceutical, auto, tire, and consumer-goods makers)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped them of the ability to seal court records and settlement evidence of public health or safety hazards, and would have guaranteed that such information could reach regulators. Because the bill died, they keep the ability to settle lawsuits under permanent secrecy.

Lawyers and consultants who manage protective orders and confidential settlements would have faced new findings requirements and reporting carve-outs. The bill's death preserves the existing framework.
The bill would have guaranteed that information relevant to a civil case could be disclosed to agencies with enforcement authority, with confidentiality protections of its own.
